review_basis: Original 2048x1152 SAP Module 02 WebP slides 09–22 visually inspected. Each scene follows displayed system flow, examples and operational constraints.
part_title: Cross-Account Resource Sharing and Transit Gateway Routing

scenes.title: AWS RAM: share resources without duplicating ownership
scenes.visual_overview: An owner account creates an AWS RAM resource share for supported infrastructure; internal participants and accepted external accounts receive defined usage, not ownership.
visual_walkthrough: Account A owns a Transit Gateway or a supported subnet and controls its lifecycle
The middle RAM share selects resources, principals and managed share permissions
Accounts B and C can gain supported use inside the organization; eligible external accounts may need an invitation
For subnet sharing, the owner controls VPC networking and participants can create permitted resources without owning the VPC
IAM principal permissions and share permissions are separate, as are service-specific billing responsibilities.
Conclude: AWS RAM extends controlled use of a supported resource while the original owning account retains operations and lifecycle authority.
scenes.visual_example: Account A owns a Transit Gateway or a supported subnet and controls its lifecycle. The middle RAM share selects resources, principals and managed share permissions. Accounts B and C can gain supported use inside the organization; eligible external accounts may need an invitation. For subnet sharing, the owner controls VPC networking and participants can create permitted resources without owning the VPC. scenes.visual_synthesis: AWS RAM extends controlled use of a supported resource while the original owning account retains operations and lifecycle authority.
scenes.narration: This diagram shows how AWS Resource Access Manager shares supported resources without transferring ownership. Begin in Account A on the left. It owns a Transit Gateway or a subnet and remains responsible for configuration, lifecycle and operational management. Follow the arrow into the RAM resource share. The owner selects which resource to share, who may use it, and the managed permissions governing permitted actions. On the right, Accounts B and C are participants in the same organization. They may use the shared resource according to that configuration, but they do not become its owners. An eligible account outside the organization can also participate where the resource type supports external sharing and the invitation is accepted. At the bottom, the VPC subnet example makes ownership concrete. A participant may create approved resources inside a shared subnet, yet it cannot take over the VPC or its route tables. IAM permissions for the participant are distinct from RAM share permissions. Check service-specific billing before assuming who pays.

scenes.title: Transit Gateway sharing and network ownership
scenes.visual_overview: A central network account owns the Transit Gateway and its route tables; app accounts create their VPC attachments and routes for east-west connectivity.
visual_walkthrough: App A's VPC uses a route entry for 10.1.0.0/16 targeting its Transit Gateway attachment
The central network account owns TGW route-table association and propagation
App B's VPC has a reciprocal route back to 10.0.0.0/16
Each participant creates supported attachments and maintains its own VPC routing; IAM/RAM share permissions, security groups, NACLs and DNS also matter
Sharing does not automatically connect networks or insert routes.
Conclude: A shared Transit Gateway requires explicit attachments, bidirectional routing and controlled propagation; ownership remains with the network account.
scenes.visual_example: App A's VPC uses a route entry for 10.1.0.0/16 targeting its Transit Gateway attachment. The central network account owns TGW route-table association and propagation. App B's VPC has a reciprocal route back to 10.0.0.0/16. Each participant creates supported attachments and maintains its own VPC routing; IAM/RAM share permissions, security groups, NACLs and DNS also matter. Sharing does not automatically connect networks or insert routes.
scenes.visual_synthesis: A shared Transit Gateway requires explicit attachments, bidirectional routing and controlled propagation; ownership remains with the network account.
scenes.narration: This architecture shows a Transit Gateway shared from a central network account to application accounts using AWS RAM. Start on the left with App A's VPC, 10.0.0.0 slash sixteen. Its route table sends traffic for App B's 10.1.0.0 slash sixteen network to the Transit Gateway attachment. Follow the arrow into the middle network account. That account owns the Transit Gateway and controls the TGW route tables, attachment associations and propagation. The gateway forwards the packet toward App B's attachment on the right. App B must also have a route back to App A's address range. The bottom flow repeats those four steps from App A to App B. Notice the ownership table: participant accounts create and manage their own VPC attachments and VPC route tables when permitted, but the network owner governs the central gateway. RAM sharing by itself creates no attachments or routes. Security groups, NACLs and DNS remain relevant, and pricing includes attachment and data processing dimensions.
